Telangana-based tech companies raised $726 million in funding during the first nine months of 2026 (9M 2026), marking a 266 per cent increase from $199 million in the year-ago period and a 12 per cent rise from $647 million in 9M 2024, according to a Tracxn report.
Advt
However, the number of funding rounds declined 30 per cent to 73 from 105 a year earlier, according to the Telangana Tech – 9M 2026 Report by Tracxn, which tracks funding, investors, exits, unicorns and city-level activity between January 1 and September 30, 2026.
According to the report, most of the fresh capital flowed into a handful of large early-stage funding rounds, led by data centre company CtrlS , as well as enterprise infrastructure businesses based in Hyderabad.

The Fiduciary Architecture of Frontier AI Defense
Enterprise boards are pressing CFOs to fund generative and autonomous AI initiatives to drive margin expansion, yet the underlying risk economics have shifted dramatically. Frontier cyber capabilities are doubling every five months, compressing exploit windows from 55 days to mere hours.
Simultaneously, cyber insurers are capping AI-related losses at 10% of policy limits, while maintaining 80+ fragmented security vendors is actively eroding operating margins. Defending against machine-speed threats with manual, siloed processes is financially unsustainable and creates unquantified balance-sheet exposure.

However, deal activity declined, with both seed- and early-stage funding rounds falling from the year-ago period. Exit activity remained limited, while the period saw the emergence of one new unicorn, space launch company Skyroot Aerospace .
Top 10 deals drive funding
The ten largest funding rounds raised $664 million, accounting for 91 per cent of Telangana's total funding of $726 million in 9M 2026. Hyderabad-based data centre company CtrlS led the list with a $423 million Series B round in June, backed by CPP Investments.
Advt
The deal alone accounted for 58 per cent of total funding and 80 per cent of the $527 million increase over 9M 2025.
CtrlS also raised $28.2 million in a Series A round in February, taking its total funding during the period to $451 million.
Skyroot Aerospace raised $60 million in a Series C round in May, while Edubuk secured $50 million in a Series B round in March. Despite the increase in capital raised, Series A and later-stage rounds declined 18 per cent to 23 from 28. The number of first-time funded companies also fell 31 per cent to 20 from 29.
Advt
Early-stage funding surged 334 per cent to $622 million from $143 million in 9M 2025, accounting for 86 per cent of the total, said the report.
The CtrlS Series B round alone contributed 68 per cent of early-stage funding. However, the number of early-stage rounds declined 27 per cent to 19.
According to Trcxn, late-stage funding rose 426 per cent to $78.1 million from $14.8 million, across four rounds

Unsiloed AI Raises $7.5 Mn Led By Felicis To Make Documents Computable
Unsiloed AI, a San Francisco-based startup founded by IIT Kharagpur batchmates Aman Mishra and Adnan Abbas, has raised $7.5 million in a seed round led by Felicis.
The company builds software that turns complex documents into structured data that AI agents can use.
What the Product Does
The Unsiloed AI platform builds APIs that let software read, extract and update information inside PDFs, presentations, Word files, scanned forms, tables, charts and images.
Read More: Vedas Agro Foods Strengthens Agricultural Sourcing and B2B Supply Network Across India
The output is structured Markdown or JSON that large language models and AI agents can work with. The company’s stated goal is to make documents “as computable as databases”.
Read More: Humyn Labs Raises $47 Mn Series A To Build Real-World Data For Robots
The platform handles parsing, extraction, classification, splitting and editing. Is used across financial services, insurance, healthcare and legal work.
Why Provenance Is the Selling Point
Unsiloed AI cites where in the original document each extracted data point came from, so a customer can check and audit the result.
That single feature decides enterprise adoption. A bank cannot act on a number pulled from a scanned statement unless it can trace the number back to the page.
Pricing starts at one cent per page. Is low enough for high-volume processing and predictable enough for a budget line.
Unsiloed AI supports private cloud, on-premises and fully air-gapped deployments.
Air-gapped support is unusual and expensive to build. It matters for defence contractors, hospitals and insurers that cannot send documents to an external API even under contract.
That capability also positions Unsiloed against cheaper extraction tools that only run in the cloud.
The Founder’s Thesis
“We believe AI agents will eventually read and write more documents than humans,” chief executive Aman Mishra said.
He argued that agents do not just need better OCR. They need a dynamic interface to read, update and act on unstructured data. That building this interface is what makes documents computable.
That framing is a step beyond document extraction. Reading a document is a one-way job; updating it means writing back into a system of record without breaking it.
What the Money Buys
Unsiloed will use the funding to advance its document models, grow its engineering team and expand cloud and on-premises deployments for enterprise customers.
Mishra said the money will also go towards hiring researchers, building a larger sales effort and creating proprietary datasets to improve the technology.
That mix is telling. A seed round that funds sales as well as research means the company already has paying enterprise customers to serve.
Document processing is one of the few AI categories where customers can measure return directly. The alternative is a team of people retyping invoices.
That makes the sales cycle shorter than most enterprise software. Is why Unsiloed can spend seed money on sales as well as research.
The hard part is the long tail of formats. Every industry has documents that no public training set covers, from Indian land records to hospital discharge summaries.

Published 6:18 PM Nov 20, 2026 Source Suehyeon Lee

JPMorgan said Bitcoin's average mining cost is about $86,000 , and that the widening gap with the current Bitcoin price is increasing pressure on miners' profitability.
It said miners facing high mining costs may have sold their Bitcoin holdings , potentially deepening the recent Bitcoin price decline .
It said spot ETFs for Bitcoin and Ether, along with leveraged ETFs , saw large retail-led net outflows , while a decline in stablecoin market capitalization pointed to money leaving the crypto market.

Photo: Shutterstock
Bitcoin's slide far below the cost of mining could intensify selling pressure from miners, JPMorgan said.
The Block reported on November 20 that JPMorgan, in a recent report, estimated Bitcoin's average mining cost at about $86,000. With Bitcoin falling below $60,000, the gap between the market price and mining cost has widened to more than $26,000.
A JPMorgan team led by Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou wrote in a November 18 report that Bitcoin was trading at about $65,000 at the time, roughly $21,000 below the estimated mining cost. Bitcoin has fallen further since then, adding to pressure on miners' profitability.
JPMorgan said miners with high costs may have sold some of their Bitcoin holdings to fund operations or raise cash for a shift into artificial intelligence businesses. That selling may have helped deepen Bitcoin's recent decline.
Still, the bank said the gap between mining costs and market prices could narrow over time. If less profitable miners leave the network, hash rate would fall and mining difficulty would adjust, reducing the gap between price and production cost.
Money has also continued to leave crypto exchange-traded funds. JPMorgan said spot Bitcoin and Ether ETFs, along with leveraged ETFs tied to Strategy, recorded large net outflows in October and November. Outflows over the past two weeks were larger than in the previous four-week period.
JPMorgan said retail investors were likely the main drivers of those withdrawals because institutional positions in Chicago Mercantile Exchange futures remained relatively stable. Bitcoin futures positions edged lower, while Ether positions stayed comparatively elevated.
By contrast, equity ETFs drew inflows. JPMorgan said retail investors may have sold crypto ETFs to buy dips in the stock market. The bank added that a decline in stablecoin market capitalization signaled that some money had left the crypto market itself.
